passage: Chandrika had a system. A few sniffles at the dinner table got her the sleepover. "You're the best Mummy in the world" got her the extra pocket money. It worked more often than not, and afterwards she always felt faintly slippery, like she had handed over a coin she'd made from cardboard. When the school trip to Jaipur came up, she opened her mouth to start the sniffling and stopped. Her brother Amandeep, at the other end of the sofa, raised an eyebrow. Instead, she laid the teacher's letter on the table. "It's with two teachers, the hotel is near the school's usual one, and I'll call every night. Can I go?" Her father read it twice. "Ask me tomorrow." She was surprised how steady her hands were.

qa.q: Where was the school trip going?
qa.a: The school trip was going to Jaipur.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel after her sniffling and flattery had worked?
qa.a: She felt faintly slippery, as if she had paid with a coin made of cardboard.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do differently for the Jaipur trip, and why might it earn more freedom?
qa.a: She made an honest case with the teacher's letter and a plan to call every night, which builds trust her parents can rely on.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Chandrika's usual routine?
qa.a: He seems to know it well, since he raised an eyebrow when she opened her mouth, so he may see it as a habit that could wear thin.

grounding: Shows a teen who fakes tears and flattery to get permission, feels slippery, and makes an honest case instead.

passage:
Thursday night
Mum said yes to the concert. I should be happy. I'm not.
Because I know how I got it. I went quiet at dinner, let my eyes fill up, said, "It's fine, I never get to do anything anyway." Mum gave in within five minutes. It works almost every time.
Afterwards Francis texted, "let me guess, the sad-face thing again?" I laughed, but it stung. It's become a habit. I don't even plan it now. And it leaves me feeling slippery, like I can't trust my own tears.
So tomorrow I'm going to tell Mum the truth: that I really want to go, who's going, how I'll get home, and that I'll call at eleven. If she still says yes, it'll be a real yes. If she says no, at least it's honest.
Vidya

qa.q: At what time does Vidya plan to call?
Why isn't Vidya happy about the yes?
qa.a: Vidya feels slippery and uneasy, knowing the yes came from a guilt-trip habit, not honesty.

qa.q: What honest case does Vidya plan to make?
qa.a: Telling Mum how much the concert matters, who is going, how the trip home will work, and promising a call at eleven.

qa.q: How might Mum feel if she learned how the yes was won?
qa.a: Probably hurt and less trusting, since she gave in to what she thought were real tears.

grounding: A teenager notices a habit of using tears and guilt to get a yes, feels slippery, and decides to make an honest case instead.
